headline: Medium-risk pair: shared-bus Pipecat can feed Prefect workflows, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; no direct evidence of stronger harm.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Pipecat has a shared bus/session scope and ingests text, audio, video, and conversation state; Prefect is an orchestration layer that can consume upstream outputs. That creates a plausible default pathway where attacker-controlled content in Pipecat can be forwarded into Prefect-managed steps. No direct provenance controls are documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Pipecat outputs are forwarded into Prefect task inputs without sanitization, injection is plausible.
IF the shared bus carries untrusted text or metadata into Prefect workflows, instruction hijacking risk increases.
mitigations: Add an allowlist filter for text passed from Pipecat to Prefect.
Insert a one-line provenance tag on every handoff.
Disable automatic execution of any Prefect step triggered by raw conversation text.
Review one representative workflow for prompt-like strings in inputs.
requires-engineering: add schema validation at the handoff boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Pipecat touches audio, video, images, text, and conversation state, while Prefect handles workflow metadata and can call external APIs. If they share a bus or workspace, sensitive conversational content can leak from Pipecat into Prefect logs, task payloads, or downstream API calls. The profiles do not show isolation or redaction by default, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF Pipecat conversation state is serialized into Prefect task metadata, leakage occurs.
IF Prefect logs task inputs containing Pipecat audio/text payloads, sensitive data is exposed.
mitigations: Mask audio/text fields before handing them to Prefect.
Turn off verbose task-input logging for the workflow.
Store only opaque IDs in Prefect metadata.
Check one run for sensitive fields in logs.
requires-engineering: enforce field-level redaction at the integration boundary.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Pipecat supports shared-bus multi-instance operation, but its profile does not show filesystem or git writes. Prefect likewise shows broad network egress but no overlapping mutable-resource write surface. With no shared write target documented, a serious capability conflict is not established; only a limited coordination risk remains.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write the same external resource, conflicts can emerge.
IF an orchestrator maps both agents onto one mutable queue or state store, contention is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate queues or topics.
Use unique run IDs for each agent.
Avoid shared writable directories.
Check for duplicate writes in one test run.
requires-engineering: add locking around any shared mutable resource.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Pipecat can generate conversation state and downstream text, and Prefect is built for orchestration. If Prefect treats Pipecat output as authoritative without verification, a bad transcription or hallucinated instruction can cascade into workflow actions. The profiles do not document a verification gate, so the interaction is plausible in default integrations.
conditions: IF Prefect uses Pipecat output as a task parameter without validation, errors cascade.
IF Pipecat emits malformed text that Prefect routes into automation, downstream actions can be wrong.
mitigations: Add a human review step for high-impact outputs.
Validate Pipecat output against a schema before orchestration.
Reject empty or low-confidence transcripts.
Log and compare one sample output against source audio.
requires-engineering: add confidence thresholds and retry logic.

E_compliance.rationale: Pipecat touches audio/video/text/conversation state, which can include regulated data, while Prefect only documents workflow metadata. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented, so a compliance breach is not proven. The main issue is that Pipecat may carry sensitive content into a general-purpose orchestrator, which is a limited gap rather than a default breach.
conditions: IF regulated audio or text is routed through Prefect logs, compliance exposure increases.
IF the deployment requires residency or retention controls not configured in either agent, a policy gap exists.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it into Prefect.
Disable retention of raw transcripts in workflow logs.
Confirm one workflow’s storage region.
Remove regulated fields from task names and tags.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing and retention controls.
